cells.tense: You are here at the bench right now, and the practice is carrying itself.
cells.ask: Let one person watch a full session this week, unedited from start to finish.
cells.core:
You sit down and it happens. No wrestling it into gear, no negotiating at the edge of the chair. The repeated thing has become something your hands know, and that ease is buying you a view you couldn't have bought any other way — you catch the whole shape of a situation, its grain and its joins, because you've been close to it long enough to stop guessing.

The quiet and the wide look are one move now. Going off alone doesn't cut you off from people; it's what makes you able to read them straight. Time by yourself used to read like a door closing. It reads like a perch now, and the perch is doing the work.

You're free to spend that on someone who's been waiting for you to come back out.
cells.sheetLine: The quiet work is what lets you see the whole shape.
cells.verb: keeping a thing lit by hand until it holds without you
cells.place: standing a step outside the whole thing and still inside it

cells.tense: You will fix one more thing before you let this one be finished.
cells.ask: Finish one thing at the level it already sits at, and leave the next correction for tomorrow.
cells.core:
There is a version of this that's finally right, and you're working toward it instead of working here. Every session turns into a correction and the correction turns into another one, and the light stays one shade shy of good enough to set down. Staying alone stops being a choice and starts being the only way you can keep going. Refining has become the thing you do instead of the thing you finish.

Here's what it costs. You can't see a whole shape while you're sanding its edge — the wide look this practice gives you is the exact look that goes missing. You see the flaw, then the flaw in the fix.

The work is real. What's absent is an endpoint. Some things you keep shoring up will fall on their own, and what comes after that isn't a loss.

cells.tense: You were at that door once, and you have not come back through it.
cells.ask: Sit with one small repeated thing for ten minutes, stop on purpose, and note what it gave you.
cells.core:
Sitting down to the repeated thing stopped being neutral a while back. So you don't sit. This isn't laziness and it isn't a missing gift — it's something that learned to stay away, and it learns well. The ability is still in you. It just doesn't have a floor under it right now, and without that floor, the wide look you're known for runs thin. You can still see parts. Whole shapes take hours in one place, and hours in one place are what you haven't been able to give.

Something smaller and fairer than pushing at the old door: one thing in, one thing out, no accounting kept. Ten minutes given, whatever it hands you taken. That's the whole exchange for today, and it's enough.
cells.sheetLine: You stopped sitting down, and the wide view went with it.

cells.tense: You are practicing right now and calling it something other than practice.
cells.ask: Tell one person who already knows you that a thing you're good at was built, not given.
cells.core:
You already do the repeated thing, and you've done it a long time in small stretches nobody watches. It shows. You handle what other people find hard, and when it comes up you wave it off — just how it is, been able to do it as long as you can remember. The practice is real. The claim on it is missing. And the wide look that comes with it, the one where you read a whole situation at once and know what's true across its layers, gets filed as something you were born holding.

You weren't. You built it the slow way, behind a shut door, one sitting at a time.

Until you say so, the skill feels like something that happened to you instead of something you did — and that can't be trusted or handed to anyone.
cells.sheetLine: You built this slowly. You keep calling it something you were born with.

attempts.check: The record's Too Much line says isolation feels necessary and refinement is compulsive, but it doesn't say what the person fears. My draft named the fear for them — 'bracing for the day it stops holding' — which oversteps the status into their interior. A reader could reasonably say 'I'm not afraid, I just have high standards and I finish things,' and the Too Much cell must survive that without arguing. The asks survive a wrong read because each is one visible act with a finish, doable today with no one else's cooperation. The sentence that serves me more than them is the steady small light — it's the card's own poetry, so I keep the plain mechanism and hand the switch to them.
